# Properties of Types and Objects

- A Data Type defines the kind of values that can be stored, operations that can be performed, and memory required.
- Elementary Data Types are Integer, Real/Floating Point, Character, and Boolean.
- Properties of Data Types:
  - Domain: set of values a type can store (e.g., Boolean → {True, False})
  - Range: minimum and maximum values allowed (e.g., 8-bit signed integer: -128 to +127)
  - Size: amount of memory required (e.g., char → 1 byte, int → 4 bytes)
  - Operations: permitted operations on the type (e.g., for integers: +, -, *, /, %)
- Properties of Objects:
  - Name: identifier used to access the object
  - Type: determines the kind of data stored
  - Value: current data stored in the object
  - Address: memory location where the object is stored
  - Lifetime: duration for which the object exists in memory
  - Scope: region of the program where the object can be accessed
- Importance of Data Types:
  - Efficient memory usage
  - Error detection
  - Type safety
  - Better program reliability
  - Faster execution
- Common Elementary Data Types:
  - Integer: stores whole numbers
  - Floating Point: stores decimal numbers
  - Character: stores a single character
  - Boolean: stores logical values
- Exam Point: Elementary Data Types are the basic data types such as Integer, Float, Character, and Boolean.

# Scalar and Composite Data Types

- A Scalar Data Type is a data type that can store only a single value at a time.
- Characteristics of Scalar Data Types: represents one value, cannot be divided into smaller components, simple and basic data types, directly operated upon by the processor.
- Examples of Scalar Data Types: Integer, Float, Character, Boolean.
- Advantages of Scalar Data Types: simple to use, fast processing, requires less memory management.
- A Composite Data Type is a data type that is formed by combining two or more scalar data items into a single unit.
- Characteristics of Composite Data Types: can store multiple values, consists of different or similar data types, used to represent complex data structures.
- Examples of Composite Data Types: Array, Structure, Record, Class.
- Features of Scalar vs Composite Data Types: values stored, complexity, components, memory requirement.
- Scalar Data Types store a single value at a time, while Composite Data Types store multiple values in a single variable.
- Examples of Scalar Data Types: int x = 10, stores only one value: 10.
- Examples of Composite Data Types: int numbers[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40}, stores multiple values in a single variable.
- Types of Composite Data Types: Array, Structure, Record, Class.
- Characteristics of Array: collection of similar data elements.
- Characteristics of Structure: collection of different data types.
- Characteristics of Record: stores related fields together.
- Characteristics of Class: used in Object-Oriented Programming.
- Examples of Array: int marks[5] = {70, 80, 90, 85, 75}.
- Examples of Structure: struct Student { int id; char name[20]; float marks; }.
- Examples of Record: Student Record - Roll Number, Name, Marks.
- Examples of Class: class Student { int id; String name; }.
- Exam Point: Scalar Data Types store a single value at a time, while Composite Data Types store multiple values in a single variable.
